topic: continual learning; LLM fine-tuning; rehearsal/memory budgets; forgetting metrics
status: bounded research-design lead from three lexical-priority full texts in one 2020-2024 topic-period cell; not a prevalence estimate or novelty claim
claim: Across these three sampled studies, conclusions about the stability–plasticity trade-off depend on both historical-data access and the chosen retention endpoint. A replay-free online visual protocol, a replay-based LLM method, and a replay-free LoRA subspace method cannot be ranked from their headline results: they use different streams, models, and forgetting measures. The evidence motivates a within-benchmark experiment that varies replay allowance and reports common old-task and new-task outcomes, while treating output-change proxies separately.
positive_evidence: Lifelong Wandering uses a one-example-at-a-time stream and excludes replay on storage/privacy realism grounds. In its own RoamingRooms protocol, OAP has lower reported forgetting than CPM (5.91 vs 31.11) at somewhat lower online accuracy (69.23 vs 73.26); LwF reaches low forgetting (2.38) but lower online accuracy (56.03).

I-LoRA stores historical examples and mixes them with current-task samples while using fast/slow LoRA learners. It leads the reported average-accuracy table on seven of eight listed Llama-2-7B domain task columns, but its BWT is still negative on seven of eight sequences and it is not best on MeetingBank.

CLoRA avoids historical-example replay and constrains LoRA update subspaces. Its separate T5-large continual table gives 79.0 vs O-LoRA's 75.8 on one benchmark, but 68.1 vs 69.6 on a larger-task benchmark; the paper's parameter/output-change forgetting proxy is not equivalent to old-task accuracy or BWT.

CLoRA's one-stage results also show that larger regularization size k is not uniformly better: reported commonsense results trend upward across tested k values while math results peak at k=128 and decline at k=256.
counterevidence: Within its own online stream, OAP demonstrates that replay-free methods can achieve a useful accuracy-retention balance; this does not imply replay is never beneficial on other tasks.

I-LoRA and CLoRA report strong results within their stated LLM evaluations, including cases where they outperform relevant baselines; metric and memory differences do not invalidate those bounded claims.
CLoRA's results across multiple task orders show it can perform strongly on a conventional continual-learning benchmark; the one large-task reversal does not establish that it is generally weak.
The three studies differ in modality, backbone, task count, data, and evaluation protocol. They cannot establish a causal effect of memory budget or a field-wide method ranking.

falsifiable_test: On one fixed LLM, task sequence, and evaluation set, compare sequential fine-tuning, I-LoRA-style replay, and CLoRA/O-LoRA-style replay-free regularization at historical-data budgets of zero, small, and larger buffers. Match current-task examples, trainable parameters, optimizer steps, and accelerator-time budgets as closely as possible; repeat seeds and task orders. Report per-task old/new accuracy, BWT/forgetting, incoming-task learning, buffer bytes/privacy exposure, training/inference cost, and parameter/output-change proxies as distinct outcomes. The lead is weakened if the same method remains best on retention and adaptation across buffer budgets under common old-task metrics; it is strengthened if rankings or the retention/plasticity frontier change systematically with memory allowance. Not run in this audit.
limitations: Only three purposively retrieved lexical-priority records from one topic-period cell; one is a vision benchmark and two are LLM studies. No common method was rerun, no cross-paper effect sizes were pooled, and no broad citation/prevalence search was completed. I-LoRA's table caption says nine benchmarks while listing eight task columns; the discrepancy is preserved rather than silently resolved. The proposed experiment is a research lead, not a novelty or causal claim.
